extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in narratology and dramatic/plot devices
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and use of anagnorisis (recognition) as a narrative device across tragedy, comedy, mystery, and modern media; explains its definition, functions, examples, and typical mechanisms of revelation. Useful for analyzing or crafting plots that hinge on sudden discovery or recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of anagnorisis
rubrics_metrics.description: A moment in a play or other work when a character makes a critical discovery; originally meant recognition in Greek context, not only of a person but also of what that person stood for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: 'a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between the persons destined by the poet for good or bad fortune' (Poetics 1452a). Emphasizes sudden awareness of a real situation, realization of things as they stood, and insight into a relationship (often with an antagonistic character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis as discovery of identity or true character (Aristotelian tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy, anagnorisis is often the discovery of one's own identity or true character, or of someone else's identity or true nature, by the tragic hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples: Oedipus learning he has killed his father and married his mother; Cordelia, Edgar, Edmund in King Lear; Electra recognizing Orestes. Aristotle considered plots that incorporate such recognition (often with peripeteia) superior to simple plots without them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis linked to peripeteia and catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Anagnorisis typically functions together with peripeteia (reversal of circumstances) and contributes to catharsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle discussed peripeteia in Poetics and defined anagnorisis as linked to it; peripeteia can be caused by anagnorisis. The combination is a mark of complex, superior tragic plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis as a marker of complex (superior) plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots that include anagnorisis (and peripeteia) are regarded as more complex and superior to simple plots that lack recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts Oedipus (complex) with Medea (simple): Medea's action involves no recognition/reversal and is thus a simpler form of plot. Use presence/absence of recognition as an evaluative criterion for plot complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition mechanisms (tokens/evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition scenes are often achieved via concrete tokens or evidentiary signs that trigger identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Aeschylus' Choephoroi): Electra recognizes Orestes by a lock of hair on the grave, identical footprints, and a piece of weaving she embroidered. In New Comedy and romances, birth tokens are a standard device for revealing true identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis in comedy (final revelation enabling happy ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: In comedy, recognition often takes the form of a final revelation (e.g., by birth tokens) that restores social order and enables marriage/happy resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New Comedy standard plot: heroine revealed to be of respectable birth so suitable to marry the hero; the tricky slave commonly engineers the revelation. Examples: The Winter's Tale (Perdita revealed as a king's daughter), The Comedy of Errors (twins recognize each other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis used as twist device in mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition can provide the critical twist or revelation in a murder mystery or detective tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earliest cited example: 'The Three Apples' (Arabian Nights) where the protagonist only discovers the culprit (his slave) at the last moment. Use of late discovery to reframe preceding events is a hallmark of mystery twist endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern cinematic usage of anagnorisis (genre-expanding examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary film and popular culture frequently employ recognition-style revelations to produce dramatic twists or shifts in audience understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Sixth Sense (protagonist realizes he is dead), Unbreakable (character realizes he survived due to supernatural power), The Empire Strikes Back (Darth Vader revealed as Luke's father). These demonstrate that anagnorisis can function beyond classical theatre, across genres, and can concern characters' knowledge of their own state or destiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of recognition (who/what may be recognized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition need not be limited to identifying a person; it can include realizing what a person stands for, the truth of a situation, or the nature of a relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotelian usage and later criticism emphasize recognition of identity, true nature, role in fate/good-or-bad fortune, or insight into relationships with antagonists; this broader scope informs how recognition functions dramaturgically.
